notes.meaning: God looks back to the early days when Israel was a young nation enslaved in Egypt. He loved them like a father loves a child, adopted them, and rescued them from slavery. Although Matthew's Gospel later shows how Jesus fulfilled this as God's true Son, Hosea first reminds the people of how tenderly God cared for them from the start.

differ.view: Some Baptist commentators hold that this verse refers primarily and directly to Jesus Christ rather than the nation of Israel, viewing the Exodus as only a picture of Christ coming out of Egypt.

notes.meaning: God repeatedly sent prophets to urge the people to turn back to Him. Instead of listening, the Israelites ran farther away from God and worshiped the false Canaanite gods called Baals. The more God reached out, the more stubborn their rebellion became.

The Lord pictures Himself as a patient parent teaching a toddler to walk. He held Israel by the arms to steady their steps and protected them from harm. Yet the people were blind to His care and never gave Him credit for healing and sustaining them.

God guided His people with kindness and human understanding rather than treating them like stubborn animals. Like a caring farmer who lifts a heavy wooden harness off an ox's neck so it can rest, God freed Israel from slavery and stooped down to feed them in the desert.

Because Israel refused to turn away from their sins, they would face harsh captivity under the king of Assyria. This new exile would be just as bitter as their ancient slavery in Egypt. Their downfall came entirely from their refusal to return to the Lord.

An enemy army would sweep through their cities with the sword, smashing through strong gate bars and city defenses. Israel trusted in human schemes and political alliances rather than God, and those very plans would destroy them.

The people were entirely set on drifting away from the Lord. Even when they called out to God during hard times, their words were empty and insincere. Because they did not truly honor Him from the heart, He would not lift their heavy burdens.

God expresses deep sorrow at the thought of abandoning His people. Admah and Zeboiim were neighbor cities of Sodom that were wiped out forever, but God could not bear to bring total destruction on Israel. His intense love and mercy held back the full punishment their sins deserved.

The Lord declares that He will not destroy Ephraim completely in burning anger. Unlike humans, who often act out of revenge or spite, God is perfectly holy and keeps His covenant promises. His holy nature blends deep justice with unmatched mercy.

One day the scattered people will turn and follow the Lord. He will call them with a mighty, commanding voice like the roar of a lion. When He calls, His children will hurry back with eager, reverent fear from lands across the western sea.

Exiled Israelites will fly back as quickly and eagerly as startled birds and doves from places like Egypt and Assyria. The Lord promises that He will safely bring them home and settle them in their own land again.

The northern kingdom of Israel surrounded God with hypocritical worship and empty promises. By contrast, the southern kingdom of Judah still maintained genuine temple worship and remained loyal to the holy God at that time.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars place this verse at the start of chapter 12, translating the Hebrew to mean that Judah was also unruly and wandering away from God, rather than faithful.
